decks.title: Compound interest — Part 1: How the amount grows
goals: Explain how compound interest differs from simple interest
Find the amount and compound interest year by year for 2 or 3 years
Use the formula for the amount and for the compound interest
Handle half-yearly compounding and different rates in successive years

slides.heading: Compound Interest, Part 1
slides.body_md: Interest that earns interest of its own.

nodes.label: Next year the larger principal earns interest

visual.alt: Flow chart of compound interest: the principal earns interest for a year, the interest is added to the principal, and the larger principal earns interest in the next year, again and again.
visual.caption: Interest on interest.

slides.narration: Welcome to compound interest. When a bank adds your interest to your money at the end of each year, the next year it pays interest on the bigger sum. Interest earns interest. In this part we learn how to work out the amount, first year by year, then with a short formula.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Work out the amount **year by year**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. We begin with the idea, build the answer one year at a time so that you can see exactly what is happening, and then replace the long working with one neat formula. Finally we change the compounding period and the rate.

slides.heading: Simple interest and compound interest
slides.body_md: With **simple interest** every year is charged on the **original** principal. With **compound interest** the interest is **added** to the principal each year, so the principal grows.

visual.alt: Table for 10000 rupees at 10 per cent a year: with simple interest the amounts are 11000, 12000 and 13000 rupees after 1, 2 and 3 years; with compound interest they are 11000, 12100 and 13310 rupees.
visual.caption: The two agree in year $1$, then compound interest pulls ahead.

slides.narration: With simple interest the interest is the same every year, because it is always worked out on the original sum. With compound interest, the interest is added to the sum at the end of each year. So the principal grows, and the interest grows with it. Look at ten thousand rupees at ten per cent. After three years, simple interest gives thirteen thousand, compound gives thirteen thousand three hundred and ten.

slides.heading: Picture of the difference
slides.body_md: Both start at ₹$10000$ at $10\%$. The straight line is simple interest; the curve is compound interest.

visual.alt: Graph of the amount on 10000 rupees at 10 per cent a year against the number of years: simple interest is a straight line through 13000 rupees at 3 years and 15000 at 5 years, while compound interest is a curve bending upwards through 13310 at 3 years and 16105.10 at 5 years.
visual.caption: The gap between the line and the curve widens every year.

slides.narration: This graph shows both. Simple interest adds the same one thousand rupees every year, so it makes a straight line. Compound interest adds a little more each year, so it bends upwards. In the first year they are equal. After that the gap grows. After five years the difference is more than one thousand rupees.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: two years, year by year
slides.body_md: Find the amount and the compound interest on ₹$8000$ for $2$ years at $5\%$ per annum.

visual.alt: Year-by-year table for a principal of 8000 rupees: year 1 principal 8000, interest 400, amount 8400; year 2 principal 8400, interest 420, amount 8820 rupees.
visual.caption: Interest ₹$400$ then ₹$420$: compound interest ₹$820$.

slides.narration: In the first year the interest is five per cent of eight thousand, which is four hundred rupees. The amount is eight thousand four hundred. That amount is the principal for the second year. Five per cent of eight thousand four hundred is four hundred and twenty. The final amount is eight thousand eight hundred and twenty rupees, so the compound interest is eight hundred and twenty.

slides.heading: Quick check: the second year
slides.body_md: The second year starts with a bigger principal.
slides.narration: Find the amount at the end of the first year. That is the principal for the second year. Then take the interest on it.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: three years, year by year
slides.body_md: Find the amount and the compound interest on ₹$12500$ for $3$ years at $8\%$ per annum.

visual.alt: Year-by-year table for a principal of 12500 rupees: year 1 principal 12500, interest 1000, amount 13500; year 2 principal 13500, interest 1080, amount 14580; year 3 principal 14580, interest 1166.4, amount 15746.4 rupees.
visual.caption: Paise appear: ₹$1166.40$ in the third year.

slides.narration: The same steps repeat. Year one gives a thousand rupees of interest and an amount of thirteen thousand five hundred. Year two gives one thousand and eighty, and an amount of fourteen thousand five hundred and eighty. Year three gives one thousand one hundred and sixty six rupees and forty paise. The compound interest is three thousand two hundred and forty six rupees and forty paise.

slides.heading: Why look for a formula?
slides.body_md: Each year the amount is multiplied by the same number, $1 + \dfrac{r}{100}$, the **growth factor**.

visual.alt: Flow chart: each year multiplies the amount by the growth factor one plus r over one hundred, so after n years the amount is P times that factor to the power n.
visual.caption: One multiplication per year.

slides.narration: Look at the working again. Each year we added a percentage of the principal, which is the same as multiplying by one plus r over one hundred. At five per cent, that factor is one point zero five. So after n years the principal has been multiplied n times by the same factor. That gives a short formula.

slides.heading: The formula for the amount
slides.body_md: For $n$ years at $r\%$ per annum, compounded yearly:

visual.alt: Table of growth factors: for rates 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15 and 20 per cent it lists one plus r over 100, its square and its cube, for example 1.05, 1.1025 and 1.157625 at 5 per cent.
visual.caption: Learn the factors at $5\%$, $10\%$ and $20\%$.

slides.narration: The amount is the principal times the factor, one plus r over one hundred, raised to the power n. The compound interest is the amount minus the principal. The time n must be in years and the rate r is per year. This table lists the factors for common rates, with their squares and cubes. Learn the ones for five, ten and twenty per cent.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: using the formula
slides.body_md: Find the amount and the compound interest on ₹$16000$ for $3$ years at $5\%$ per annum.

visual.alt: Working table for 16000 rupees at 5 per cent for 3 years: the growth factor is 1.157625, the amount is 18522 rupees and the compound interest is 2522 rupees.
visual.caption: Compound interest ₹$2522$.

slides.narration: Write the formula, substitute sixteen thousand, five and three, and work out one point zero five cubed, which is one point one five seven six two five. Multiply by sixteen thousand to get eighteen thousand five hundred and twenty two rupees. Subtract the principal for the compound interest, two thousand five hundred and twenty two rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: compound interest
slides.body_md: Amount first, then subtract the principal.
slides.narration: Use the factor one point one zero two five for two years at five per cent. Find the amount, then take away the principal.

slides.heading: Half-yearly compounding
slides.body_md: If interest is **compounded half-yearly**, it is added every **six months**. **Halve the rate** and **double the time**.

visual.alt: Flow chart for half-yearly compounding: halve the yearly rate, double the number of years to get the number of half-years, then use the amount formula with these values.
visual.caption: Halve the rate, double the time.

slides.narration: Sometimes interest is added every six months. Then the year has two interest periods. The rate for each period is half the yearly rate, and the number of periods is twice the number of years. For eight per cent a year over two and a half years, we use four per cent and five periods.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: half-yearly
slides.body_md: Find the amount and the compound interest on ₹$10000$ for $1\tfrac{1}{2}$ years at $10\%$ per annum, compounded half-yearly.

visual.alt: Working table for 10000 rupees at 10 per cent a year for one and a half years compounded half-yearly: 5 per cent for each of 3 half-years, factor 1.157625, amount 11576.25 rupees and compound interest 1576.25 rupees.
visual.caption: Amount ₹$11576.25$.

slides.narration: The yearly rate is ten per cent, so each half-year earns five per cent. One and a half years is three half-years. The amount is ten thousand times one point zero five cubed, which is eleven thousand five hundred and seventy six rupees and twenty five paise. The compound interest is one thousand five hundred and seventy six rupees and twenty five paise.

slides.heading: Quick check: rate and periods
slides.body_md: Halve the rate, double the time.
slides.narration: For two and a half years compounded half-yearly, how many periods are there, and what is the rate for each?

slides.heading: Different rates in different years
slides.body_md: If the rates are $r_1\%$, $r_2\%$, $r_3\%$ in successive years, multiply the principal by **each year's** factor:
slides.narration: Sometimes a bank changes its rate from year to year. Then each year has its own growth factor. We multiply the principal by the factor for the first year, then the second, then the third. The powers are no longer used, because the factors are different. The order does not change the final amount.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: three different rates
slides.body_md: Find the amount and the compound interest on ₹$15000$ for $3$ years if the rates are $6\%$, $8\%$ and $10\%$ in the three years.

visual.alt: Table for 15000 rupees with rates 6, 8 and 10 per cent in successive years: the amounts are 15900, 17172 and 18889.20 rupees.
visual.caption: Each year uses its own rate.

slides.narration: Multiply fifteen thousand by one point zero six, then by one point zero eight, then by one point one. The factor altogether is one point two five nine two eight, and the amount is eighteen thousand eight hundred and eighty nine rupees and twenty paise. The compound interest is three thousand eight hundred and eighty nine rupees and twenty paise.

slides.heading: Quick check: half-yearly rate
slides.body_md: Is the whole yearly rate added every six months?
slides.narration: Think about what happens to the rate when the interest is added twice a year.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Year by year: the amount becomes the next principal
Compound interest is more than simple interest after year $1$

rows: amount at the end of a year = principal for the next year

visual.alt: Summary table: year by year the amount becomes the next principal; the amount formula; CI is A minus P; half-yearly halves the rate and doubles the time; different rates multiply their factors.
visual.caption: Part 1 in five lines.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. In compound interest, each year the amount becomes the principal for the next year. The amount is P times one plus r over one hundred, to the power n, and the compound interest is the amount minus the principal. For half-yearly interest halve the rate and double the time. For different rates multiply the factors.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Always** subtract $P$ when the question asks for the **interest**
**Mistake:** using simple interest for the second year
**Mistake:** not halving the rate for half-yearly interest
**Mistake:** rounding the factor early; keep it exact
slides.narration: In the exam, write the formula first, then substitute. That earns a mark even if the arithmetic slips. Three traps to avoid: using the same principal every year, which is simple interest; forgetting to halve the rate and double the time for half-yearly interest; and giving the amount when the question asks for the interest.

decks.title: Compound interest — Part 2: Inverse problems, differences, growth and depreciation
goals: Find the principal, the rate or the time from the other quantities
Find the difference between compound and simple interest
Apply the formula to population growth and bacteria
Apply it to depreciation of machines and vehicles

slides.heading: Compound Interest, Part 2
slides.body_md: Work backwards, compare, then grow and shrink.

nodes.label: Rate $r$: write $\dfrac{A}{P}$ as a perfect power
Time $n$: compare $\dfrac{A}{P}$ with powers of the factor

visual.alt: Decision chart for inverse problems: if the principal is unknown divide the amount by the growth factor; if the rate is unknown write the ratio of amount to principal as a perfect power; if the time is unknown compare the ratio with powers of the factor; always check by working forwards.
visual.caption: Three kinds of inverse problem.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. First we run the formula backwards: if we know the amount, how do we find the principal, the rate or the time? Then we compare compound interest with simple interest. Finally we use the same idea for things that grow, like populations, and things that lose value, like machines.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **difference** between CI and SI
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. The first group needs a little algebra and a lot of care. The second is a handy shortcut. The third and fourth are applications that appear in many problems about towns, cultures and machines.

slides.heading: Finding the principal
slides.body_md: The amount is $P$ times a factor, so $P$ is the amount **divided** by the factor:
slides.narration: The amount equals the principal times the growth factor. So to find the principal, divide the amount by the factor. For two years at five per cent, the factor is one point one zero two five. Do not divide by one point zero five only once, which is a common slip.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the principal
slides.body_md: A sum amounts to ₹$7938$ in $2$ years at $5\%$ per annum, compounded yearly. Find the sum.

visual.alt: Steps for finding the principal when 7938 rupees is the amount after 2 years at 5 per cent: the factor is 1.1025 and the principal is 7938 divided by 1.1025, which is 7200 rupees.
visual.caption: Principal ₹$7200$.

slides.narration: The factor for two years at five per cent is one point one zero two five. Divide seven thousand nine hundred and thirty eight by that factor to get seven thousand two hundred rupees. We check by working forwards: seven thousand two hundred times one point zero five is seven thousand five hundred and sixty, and again gives seven thousand nine hundred and thirty eight.

slides.heading: Quick check: find the principal
slides.body_md: Divide by the factor for the full two years.
slides.narration: The amount is given. Divide it by the factor for two years at five per cent, not by the factor for one year.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the rate
slides.body_md: ₹$25000$ amounts to ₹$28090$ in $2$ years, compounded yearly. Find the rate per cent.

visual.alt: Steps for finding the rate: 28090 divided by 25000 is 1.1236, which is 1.06 squared, so the factor is 1.06 and the rate is 6 per cent.
visual.caption: Rate $6\%$.

slides.narration: Divide the amount by the principal to get one point one two three six. For two years, this is the factor squared. One point one two three six is one point zero six squared. So the factor is one point zero six and the rate is six per cent a year. Check: twenty five thousand times one point zero six squared gives twenty eight thousand and ninety.

slides.heading: Finding the time
slides.body_md: Compare $\dfrac{A}{P}$ with powers of the factor until they match.

visual.alt: Table of powers of 1.2 and the amount on 5000 rupees at 20 per cent: 1.2 gives 6000, 1.44 gives 7200, 1.728 gives 8640 and 2.0736 gives 10368 rupees after 1, 2, 3 and 4 years.
visual.caption: The amount $8640$ matches $n = 3$.

slides.narration: When the time is unknown, work out the ratio of the amount to the principal and compare it with powers of the factor. For five thousand rupees at twenty per cent, the amounts after one, two, three and four years are six thousand, seven thousand two hundred, eight thousand six hundred and forty, and ten thousand three hundred and sixty eight.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the time
slides.body_md: In how many years will ₹$5000$ amount to ₹$8640$ at $20\%$ per annum, compounded yearly?

visual.alt: Table of powers of 1.2 and the amount on 5000 rupees at 20 per cent: 1.2 gives 6000, 1.44 gives 7200, 1.728 gives 8640 and 2.0736 gives 10368 rupees after 1, 2, 3 and 4 years.
visual.caption: The amount $8640$ matches $n = 3$.

slides.narration: The ratio of eight thousand six hundred and forty to five thousand is one point seven two eight. One point two cubed is exactly one point seven two eight, so the time is three years. The check by working forward is five thousand, six thousand, seven thousand two hundred, and eight thousand six hundred and forty.

slides.heading: Quick check: find the time
slides.body_md: Compare the ratio of amount to principal with powers of the factor.
slides.narration: Divide the amount by the principal. Then compare the ratio with powers of one point zero four until one of them matches.

slides.heading: Compound interest minus simple interest
slides.body_md: For the same $P$, $r$ and time, the compound interest is the larger. The difference has a shortcut:

visual.alt: Table of the difference between compound interest and simple interest: for 2 years it is P times r over 100 squared; for 3 years it is P times r over 100 squared times the sum 3 plus r over 100.
visual.caption: Learn both; check by direct working.

slides.narration: In the first year compound and simple interest are equal. For two years, the whole difference is the interest on the first year's interest, which comes to the principal times r over one hundred, squared. For three years there is a longer formula with the extra factor three plus r over one hundred. You can always find both interests and subtract.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the difference
slides.body_md: Find the difference between CI and SI on ₹$20000$ for $2$ years at $5\%$ per annum.

visual.alt: Comparison table: 20000 rupees at 5 per cent for 2 years gives compound interest 2050 and simple interest 2000, a difference of 50; 18000 rupees at 10 per cent for 2 years gives 3780 and 3600, a difference of 180.
visual.caption: The difference is small but never zero after year $1$.

slides.narration: Compound interest is twenty thousand times one point one zero two five, minus twenty thousand, which is two thousand and fifty. Simple interest is two thousand. The difference is fifty rupees. The shortcut gives the same answer: twenty thousand times five over one hundred, squared, is fifty.

slides.heading: Quick check: a three-year difference
slides.body_md: Use the three-year formula, or find CI and SI separately.
slides.narration: For three years, find the compound interest and the simple interest, then subtract. Or use the three year formula with the extra factor.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: find the sum from the difference
slides.body_md: The difference between CI and SI on a sum for $2$ years at $10\%$ per annum is ₹$180$. Find the sum.

visual.alt: Comparison table: 20000 rupees at 5 per cent for 2 years gives compound interest 2050 and simple interest 2000, a difference of 50; 18000 rupees at 10 per cent for 2 years gives 3780 and 3600, a difference of 180.
visual.caption: The difference is small but never zero after year $1$.

slides.narration: Use the two year shortcut. The difference of one hundred and eighty equals P times one hundredth, because ten per cent squared is one hundredth. So P is one hundred and eighty divided by one hundredth, which is eighteen thousand rupees. The check: compound interest three thousand seven hundred and eighty, simple interest three thousand six hundred.

slides.heading: Growth and depreciation
slides.body_md: **Growth** at $r\%$ a year multiplies by $1 + \dfrac{r}{100}$. **Depreciation** at $r\%$ a year multiplies by $1 - \dfrac{r}{100}$.

visual.alt: Graph of a population of 40000 growing 5 per cent a year compared with a straight line adding 2000 a year: after 3 years the compound growth reaches 46305 while the straight line reaches 46000.
visual.caption: Growth at a fixed rate is compounded.

slides.narration: The same idea works whenever something changes by a fixed percentage each year. A population growing at five per cent a year is multiplied by one point zero five each year. A machine losing ten per cent of its value each year is multiplied by zero point nine each year. Population answers should be whole numbers.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: population
slides.body_md: The population of a town is $40000$ and grows at $5\%$ per annum. Find the population after $3$ years.

visual.alt: Table for a population of 40000 growing 5 per cent a year: the increases are 2000, 2100 and 2205, and the populations at the end of each year are 42000, 44100 and 46305.
visual.caption: Population after $3$ years: $46305$.

slides.narration: Multiply forty thousand by one point zero five cubed, which is one point one five seven six two five. The population after three years is forty six thousand three hundred and five. Year by year it is forty two thousand, forty four thousand one hundred, and forty six thousand three hundred and five. The increase gets bigger each year.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: depreciation
slides.body_md: A machine costing ₹$50000$ depreciates at $10\%$ per annum. Find its value after $3$ years.

visual.alt: Table for a machine of 50000 rupees losing 10 per cent a year: the falls are 5000, 4500 and 4050 rupees and the values at the end of each year are 45000, 40500 and 36450 rupees.
visual.caption: The fall shrinks as the value shrinks.

slides.narration: Multiply fifty thousand by zero point nine cubed, which is zero point seven two nine. The value after three years is thirty six thousand four hundred and fifty rupees. Notice the fall each year: five thousand, then four thousand five hundred, then four thousand and fifty. The fall shrinks because ten per cent is taken of a smaller value.

slides.heading: Quick check: the same fall each year?
slides.body_md: Think about the table of falls: 5000, 4500, 4050.
slides.narration: Look at the fall in value each year in the table. Is it the same number of rupees every year, or does it change?

slides.heading: Percentage fall against fixed fall
slides.body_md: The curve is depreciation at $10\%$ a year. The straight line is a fixed fall of ₹$5000$ a year.

functions.label: loses 10% of its value a year

visual.alt: Graph of the value of a machine of 50000 rupees: losing 10 per cent a year gives a curve through 45000, 40500 and 36450 rupees; losing a fixed 5000 a year gives a straight line through 45000, 40000 and 35000 rupees. The curve falls more slowly.
visual.caption: Percentage depreciation falls more slowly than a fixed fall.

slides.narration: Compare two machines that both start at fifty thousand rupees. One loses a fixed five thousand rupees every year. The other loses ten per cent of its present value each year. After three years the first is worth thirty five thousand and the second is worth thirty six thousand four hundred and fifty. Percentage depreciation falls more slowly.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: a rise and a fall
slides.body_md: A plot of land costing ₹$80000$ rises in value by $25\%$ in one year and then falls by $20\%$ in the next year. What is its value at the end?
bullets: **Compare —** a rise and fall of the same per cent do **not** cancel.

visual.alt: Table of a rise followed by a fall: 80000 rupees rising 25 per cent becomes 100000 and falling 20 per cent returns to 80000; 10000 rupees rising 20 per cent becomes 12000 and falling 20 per cent ends at 9600.
visual.caption: Each change works on the latest value.

slides.narration: After a twenty five per cent rise, eighty thousand rupees becomes one lakh. A twenty per cent fall of one lakh is twenty thousand, giving eighty thousand again. So here the plot returns exactly to its start. But a twenty per cent rise followed by a twenty per cent fall gives ninety six per cent of the start, because each change works on the latest value.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $P = \dfrac{A}{\left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right)^{n}}$; the rate from a perfect power; the time by comparing powers
Check every answer by working forwards

rows: write $\dfrac{A}{P}$ as a perfect power; read off $1 + \dfrac{r}{100}$
compare $\dfrac{A}{P}$ with powers of the factor; check year by year

visual.alt: Summary table of part 2: dividing for the principal, a perfect power for the rate, comparing powers for the time, the difference formula for two years, and the growth and depreciation formulas.
visual.caption: Part 2 in six lines.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. Divide the amount by the factor to find the principal. Write the ratio as a perfect power to find the rate, and compare with powers to find the time. Memorise the two year difference shortcut. For growth use the factor one plus r over one hundred, and for depreciation use one minus r over one hundred.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Principal, rate or time (3–4 marks):** equation 1–2 + working 1 + answer 1
**Growth or depreciation (2–3 marks):** factor 1 + substitution 1 + answer 1
**Not in the syllabus:** repaying a loan in equal instalments
slides.narration: For inverse problems show the equation clearly and check your answer by working forwards. For depreciation, make sure you subtract in the factor, one minus r over one hundred. Populations are whole numbers. One line: repaying a loan in equal instalments is not in the I C S E two thousand twenty eight Class nine syllabus, so you do not need it.

notes.title: Compound Interest — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Simple interest and compound interest
sections.body_md:
With **simple interest** the interest is always worked out on the **original principal**, so it is the same every year. With **compound interest** the interest is **added to the principal** at the end of each period, and the next period's interest is worked out on the larger sum: interest earns interest.

- In the **first year** the two are equal.
- After that, compound interest is **more** than simple interest.
- The **amount** is $A = P + \text{interest}$ and the **compound interest** is $\text{CI} = A - P$.

key_terms.definition_md: Interest worked out on the principal plus the interest already added in earlier periods.
The principal together with the interest: $A = P + \text{interest}$.
The time after which interest is added to the principal (a year, or six months).

nodes.label: Next year the larger principal earns interest

visual.alt: Flow chart of compound interest: the principal earns interest for a year, the interest is added to the principal, and the larger principal earns interest in the next year, again and again.
visual.caption: Interest on interest.

visuals.alt: Table for 10000 rupees at 10 per cent a year: with simple interest the amounts are 11000, 12000 and 13000 rupees after 1, 2 and 3 years; with compound interest they are 11000, 12100 and 13310 rupees.
visuals.caption: The two agree in year $1$, then compound interest pulls ahead.

sections.heading: 2. Year-by-year method (no formula)
sections.body_md:
For $2$ or $3$ years make a table: **principal at the start**, **interest for the year**, **amount at the end**. The amount at the end of a year is the principal for the next year.

*Example:* ₹$8000$ at $5\%$ for $2$ years: year 1 interest $400$, amount $8400$; year 2 interest $420$, amount $8820$; $\text{CI} = 820$ (simple interest would be $800$).

*Example:* ₹$12500$ at $8\%$ for $3$ years: amounts $13500$, $14580$, $15746.40$; $\text{CI} = 3246.40$.

visual.alt: Year-by-year table for a principal of 8000 rupees: year 1 principal 8000, interest 400, amount 8400; year 2 principal 8400, interest 420, amount 8820 rupees.
visual.caption: Interest ₹$400$ then ₹$420$: compound interest ₹$820$.

visuals.alt: Year-by-year table for a principal of 12500 rupees: year 1 principal 12500, interest 1000, amount 13500; year 2 principal 13500, interest 1080, amount 14580; year 3 principal 14580, interest 1166.4, amount 15746.4 rupees.
visuals.caption: Paise appear: ₹$1166.40$ in the third year.

sections.heading: 3. The formula for the amount
sections.body_md:
Each year multiplies the amount by the **growth factor** $1 + \dfrac{r}{100}$, so for $n$ years:

$$A = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right)^{n}, \qquad \text{CI} = A - P.$$

- $n$ is in **years** and $r$ is **per annum**.
- *Example:* ₹$16000$ at $5\%$ for $3$ years: $A = 16000 \times 1.157625 = 18522$; $\text{CI} = 2522$.
- Keep the factor exact until the final multiplication.

key_terms.definition_md: The number $1 + \dfrac{r}{100}$ by which the amount is multiplied each year.

visual.alt: Flow chart: each year multiplies the amount by the growth factor one plus r over one hundred, so after n years the amount is P times that factor to the power n.
visual.caption: One multiplication per year.

visuals.alt: Table of growth factors: for rates 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15 and 20 per cent it lists one plus r over 100, its square and its cube, for example 1.05, 1.1025 and 1.157625 at 5 per cent.
visuals.caption: Learn the factors at $5\%$, $10\%$ and $20\%$.

visuals.alt: Working table for 16000 rupees at 5 per cent for 3 years: the growth factor is 1.157625, the amount is 18522 rupees and the compound interest is 2522 rupees.
visuals.caption: Compound interest ₹$2522$.

sections.heading: 4. Half-yearly compounding and different rates
sections.body_md:
**Half-yearly:** interest is added every six months. **Halve the rate and double the time:**

$$A = P\left(1 + \frac{r/2}{100}\right)^{2n}.$$

*Example:* ₹$10000$ at $10\%$ for $1.5$ years: $5\%$ for $3$ half-years, $A = 10000 \times 1.157625 = 11576.25$, $\text{CI} = 1576.25$.

**Different rates** in successive years: multiply by each year's factor, $A = P\left(1 + \dfrac{r_1}{100}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{r_2}{100}\right)\cdots$. *Example:* ₹$15000$ at $6\%$, $8\%$, $10\%$: $A = 18889.20$.

visual.alt: Flow chart for half-yearly compounding: halve the yearly rate, double the number of years to get the number of half-years, then use the amount formula with these values.
visual.caption: Halve the rate, double the time.

visuals.alt: Working table for 10000 rupees at 10 per cent a year for one and a half years compounded half-yearly: 5 per cent for each of 3 half-years, factor 1.157625, amount 11576.25 rupees and compound interest 1576.25 rupees.
visuals.caption: Amount ₹$11576.25$.

visuals.alt: Table for 15000 rupees with rates 6, 8 and 10 per cent in successive years: the amounts are 15900, 17172 and 18889.20 rupees.
visuals.caption: Each year uses its own rate.

sections.heading: 5. Finding the principal, the rate or the time
sections.body_md:
Run the formula backwards:

- **Principal:** $P = \dfrac{A}{\left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right)^{n}}$. *Example:* $A = 7938$, $5\%$, $2$ years: $P = 7200$.
- **Rate:** write $\dfrac{A}{P}$ as a perfect power: $\dfrac{28090}{25000} = 1.1236 = (1.06)^{2}$, so $r = 6$.
- **Time:** compare $\dfrac{A}{P}$ with powers of the factor: $\dfrac{8640}{5000} = 1.728 = (1.2)^{3}$, so $n = 3$.
- Always **check** by working forwards, year by year.

nodes.label: Rate $r$: write $\dfrac{A}{P}$ as a perfect power
Time $n$: compare $\dfrac{A}{P}$ with powers of the factor

visual.alt: Decision chart for inverse problems: if the principal is unknown divide the amount by the growth factor; if the rate is unknown write the ratio of amount to principal as a perfect power; if the time is unknown compare the ratio with powers of the factor; always check by working forwards.
visual.caption: Three kinds of inverse problem.

visuals.alt: Steps for finding the principal when 7938 rupees is the amount after 2 years at 5 per cent: the factor is 1.1025 and the principal is 7938 divided by 1.1025, which is 7200 rupees.
visuals.caption: Principal ₹$7200$.

visuals.alt: Steps for finding the rate: 28090 divided by 25000 is 1.1236, which is 1.06 squared, so the factor is 1.06 and the rate is 6 per cent.
visuals.caption: Rate $6\%$.

visuals.alt: Table of powers of 1.2 and the amount on 5000 rupees at 20 per cent: 1.2 gives 6000, 1.44 gives 7200, 1.728 gives 8640 and 2.0736 gives 10368 rupees after 1, 2, 3 and 4 years.
visuals.caption: The amount $8640$ matches $n = 3$.

sections.heading: 6. Difference between compound and simple interest
sections.body_md:
For the same $P$, $r$ and time:

- $1$ year: the two are **equal**.
- $2$ years: $\text{CI} - \text{SI} = P\left(\dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{2}$.
- $3$ years: $\text{CI} - \text{SI} = P\left(\dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{2}\left(3 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)$.

*Example:* ₹$20000$, $5\%$, $2$ years: $\text{CI} = 2050$, $\text{SI} = 2000$, difference $50$. If the **difference is given**, divide by $\left(\dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{2}$ to find $P$: $180 = 0.01P$ gives $P = 18000$.

visual.alt: Table of the difference between compound interest and simple interest: for 2 years it is P times r over 100 squared; for 3 years it is P times r over 100 squared times the sum 3 plus r over 100.
visual.caption: Learn both; check by direct working.

visuals.alt: Comparison table: 20000 rupees at 5 per cent for 2 years gives compound interest 2050 and simple interest 2000, a difference of 50; 18000 rupees at 10 per cent for 2 years gives 3780 and 3600, a difference of 180.
visuals.caption: The difference is small but never zero after year $1$.

visuals.alt: Graph of the amount on 10000 rupees at 10 per cent a year against the number of years: simple interest is a straight line through 13000 rupees at 3 years and 15000 at 5 years, while compound interest is a curve bending upwards through 13310 at 3 years and 16105.10 at 5 years.
visuals.caption: The gap between the line and the curve widens every year.

sections.heading: 7. Growth and depreciation
sections.body_md:
A quantity that changes by a fixed per cent each year follows the compound-interest formula.

- **Growth** (population, bacteria, savings): $N = N_0\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{n}$. *Example:* $40000$ at $5\%$ for $3$ years gives $46305$.
- **Depreciation** (machines, vehicles): $V = V_0\left(1 - \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{n}$. *Example:* ₹$50000$ at $10\%$ for $3$ years gives ₹$36450$.
- Different rates in different years: multiply the factors. A rise and a fall of the same per cent do **not** cancel: $1.2 \times 0.8 = 0.96$.
- Populations and numbers of bacteria are **whole numbers**.

key_terms.definition_md: The fall in the value of an article (a machine, a vehicle) with use and time.

visual.alt: Graph of a population of 40000 growing 5 per cent a year compared with a straight line adding 2000 a year: after 3 years the compound growth reaches 46305 while the straight line reaches 46000.
visual.caption: Growth at a fixed rate is compounded.

visuals.alt: Table for a population of 40000 growing 5 per cent a year: the increases are 2000, 2100 and 2205, and the populations at the end of each year are 42000, 44100 and 46305.
visuals.caption: Population after $3$ years: $46305$.

visuals.alt: Table for a machine of 50000 rupees losing 10 per cent a year: the falls are 5000, 4500 and 4050 rupees and the values at the end of each year are 45000, 40500 and 36450 rupees.
visuals.caption: The fall shrinks as the value shrinks.

functions.label: loses 10% of its value a year

visuals.alt: Graph of the value of a machine of 50000 rupees: losing 10 per cent a year gives a curve through 45000, 40500 and 36450 rupees; losing a fixed 5000 a year gives a straight line through 45000, 40000 and 35000 rupees. The curve falls more slowly.
visuals.caption: Percentage depreciation falls more slowly than a fixed fall.

visuals.alt: Table of a rise followed by a fall: 80000 rupees rising 25 per cent becomes 100000 and falling 20 per cent returns to 80000; 10000 rupees rising 20 per cent becomes 12000 and falling 20 per cent ends at 9600.
visuals.caption: Each change works on the latest value.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Amount or compound interest (2–3 marks):* formula 1; substitution 1; answer 1 (subtract $P$ for the interest).
- *Half-yearly (3 marks):* rate and periods 1; substitution 1; answer 1.
- *Principal, rate or time (3–4 marks):* equation 1–2; working 1; answer 1.
- *Difference between CI and SI (2–3 marks):* CI 1; SI 1; difference 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c) usually 3 + 3 + 4; show all working.

**Common mistakes**
1. Using the original principal every year (that is simple interest).
2. Not halving the rate, or not doubling the time, for half-yearly interest.
3. Giving the amount when the interest is asked (forgetting to subtract $P$).
4. Using $1 + \dfrac{r}{100}$ for depreciation, or $1 - \dfrac{r}{100}$ for growth.
5. Dividing by the factor only once to find the principal of a multi-year problem.
6. Giving a fractional population or number of bacteria.

*Scope:* repaying a loan in equal instalments is not in the ICSE 2028 Class IX syllabus.

cards.back_md: Interest worked out on the principal **plus the interest already added** in earlier periods.
The principal together with the interest: $A = P + \text{interest}$.

cards.front_md: Principal for the second year, in year-by-year working?
cards.back_md: The **amount at the end of the first year**.

cards.front_md: Compound interest and simple interest in the first year?
₹$8000$ at $5\%$ for $2$ years, year by year: CI?

cards.back_md: $1 + \dfrac{r}{100}$, the number the amount is multiplied by each year.

Different rates $r_1$, $r_2$ in successive years: amount?

Write $\dfrac{A}{P}$ as a perfect power and read off $1 + \dfrac{r}{100}$.
Compare $\dfrac{A}{P}$ with powers of the factor; check year by year.

cards.front_md: How to check an inverse answer?
cards.back_md: Work forwards: put it back into the formula or go year by year.

cards.front_md: Graph of the amount: simple against compound?
cards.back_md: A straight line against a curve bending upwards; they meet at year $1$.

cards.front_md: Does a machine losing $10\%$ a year lose the same rupees each year?
cards.back_md: No: each fall is $10\%$ of a smaller value (₹$5000$, ₹$4500$, ₹$4050$ for ₹$50000$).

questions.stem_md: Anwar deposits money for 3 years in a scheme that pays compound interest every year. The interest for the second year is calculated on

options.text_md: the original sum plus the interest of the first year
the interest of the first year only
the original sum plus the interest of all three years

questions.solution_md: In compound interest the interest earned is added to the principal at the end of each year, so the new principal for the second year is the original sum plus the first year's interest. Option (b) describes simple interest.

questions.stem_md: The amount $A$ when a sum $P$ is invested for $n$ years at $r\%$ per annum, with interest compounded yearly, is given by
questions.solution_md: Each year multiplies the principal by $1 + \dfrac{r}{100}$, so after $n$ years the amount is $P\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{n}$. Option (c) is the simple-interest amount; (a) is the formula for depreciation.

questions.stem_md: Find the amount of ₹6,000 invested for 2 years at 10% per annum, with interest compounded yearly.
questions.solution_md: $A = 6000 \times (1.1)^{2} = 6000 \times 1.21 = 7260$. Option (d) is the simple-interest amount; (a) is only the compound interest; (b) is the amount after 3 years.

questions.stem_md: Hardeep deposits ₹5,000 at 4% per annum compounded yearly. The interest for the second year is
questions.solution_md: After the first year the amount is $5000 + 200 = 5200$, and this is the principal for the second year: $5200 \times \dfrac{4}{100} = 208$. Option (a) is the first year's interest; (c) is the third year's interest.

questions.stem_md: Sunita invests ₹16,000 for one year at 10% per annum, with interest compounded half-yearly. The amount she receives is
questions.solution_md: The rate per half-year is $5\%$ and there are $2$ half-years: $A = 16000 \times (1.05)^{2} = 16000 \times 1.1025 = 17640$. Option (b) is the amount when compounded yearly; (c) is only the interest.

questions.stem_md: A sum is invested at 8% per annum for 2.5 years with interest compounded half-yearly. In the formula, the rate per period and the number of periods are
questions.solution_md: Compounded half-yearly, the yearly rate is halved: $8 \div 2 = 4\%$ per half-year; the time is doubled: $2.5 \times 2 = 5$ half-years. The other three options forget to halve the rate, to double the time, or both.

questions.stem_md: The interest rate on a savings plan is 5% for the first year and 10% for the second year, compounded yearly. The amount of ₹12,000 after the two years is
questions.solution_md: $A = 12000 \times 1.05 \times 1.10 = 13860$. Option (d) averages the rates to $7.5\%$ simple interest; (a) uses $10\%$ in both years; (b) uses $5\%$ in both years.

questions.stem_md: A sum of money amounts to ₹11,025 in 2 years at 5% per annum compounded yearly. The sum is
A sum of ₹4,000 grows to ₹4,410 in 2 years at a rate of compound interest per annum. The rate is
questions.solution_md: $4410 = 4000\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{2}$ gives $\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{2} = 1.1025 = (1.05)^{2}$, so $r = 5$. Option (b) divides the total interest $410$ the wrong way; (c) is the total percentage gain.

questions.stem_md: In how many years will ₹2,000 amount to ₹2,662 at 10% per annum compound interest?
The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on ₹12,500 for 2 years at 4% per annum is
questions.solution_md: For 2 years, difference $= P\left(\dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{2} = 12500 \times \dfrac{16}{10000} = 20$. Option (d) doubles it; (a) is the simple interest for one year.

questions.stem_md: For the same principal, rate and time of more than one year, which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The compound interest is less than the simple interest.
The compound interest is equal to the simple interest.
The compound interest is exactly double the simple interest.
The compound interest is more than the simple interest.

questions.solution_md: From the second year onwards, compound interest is earned on interest already added, so it is larger than simple interest. In the first year the two are equal, but not for a longer time.

questions.stem_md: The population of a town is 25,000. It grows at 4% per annum. Its population after 2 years is
questions.solution_md: $N = 25000 \times (1.04)^{2} = 25000 \times 1.0816 = 27040$. Option (b) adds $4\%$ of $25000$ twice (no compounding); (c) is only the increase.

questions.stem_md: A scooter bought for ₹60,000 loses 10% of its value every year. Its value after 2 years is
questions.solution_md: $V = 60000 \times (0.9)^{2} = 60000 \times 0.81 = 48600$. Option (c) takes $10\%$ of $60000$ twice; (d) uses growth instead of depreciation; (a) is the fall in value.

questions.stem_md: The value of a machine rises by 20% in one year and then falls by 20% in the next year. Over the two years its value
questions.solution_md: The value is multiplied by $1.2 \times 0.8 = 0.96$, which is $96\%$ of the original: a fall of $4\%$. The $20\%$ fall is taken on the larger value, so it removes more than the $20\%$ rise added.

questions.stem_md: Rohit invests ₹2,500 for 2 years at 6% per annum compounded yearly. The compound interest he earns is
questions.solution_md: $A = 2500 \times (1.06)^{2} = 2500 \times 1.1236 = 2809$, so $\text{CI} = A - P = 2809 - 2500 = 309$. Option (a) is the amount; (b) is the simple interest.

questions.stem_md: The compound interest on a sum for 2 years at 10% per annum is ₹2,100. The sum is
questions.solution_md: $\text{CI} = P\left[(1.1)^{2} - 1\right] = 0.21P = 2100$, so $P = 10000$. Option (b) uses $20\%$ as if the interest were simple; (c) forgets to divide by $0.21$.

questions.stem_md: The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on ₹6,000 for 3 years at 10% per annum is
questions.solution_md: $\text{CI} = 6000 \times (1.331 - 1) = 1986$ and $\text{SI} = \dfrac{6000 \times 10 \times 3}{100} = 1800$, so the difference is $186$. Option (c) is the 2-year difference; (d) forgets the $\dfrac{r}{100}$ in the 3-year formula; (a) is the compound interest.

questions.stem_md: Lakshmi puts ₹20,000 in a bank at 20% per annum for one year. How much more interest does she earn if the bank compounds half-yearly instead of yearly?
questions.solution_md: Half-yearly: $20000 \times (1.1)^{2} = 24200$, interest $4200$. Yearly: $20000 \times 1.2 = 24000$, interest $4000$. The extra interest is $4200 - 4000 = 200$. Option (d) forgets that the first half-year's interest earns interest; (b) is the yearly interest.

questions.stem_md: Tara works out the amount of ₹7,500 at 8% per annum for 2 years as $7500\left(1 + \dfrac{8 \times 2}{100}\right) = 8700$. Her mistake is that she

options.text_md: used 8 as the time and 2 as the rate
used the simple-interest formula where compound interest was needed

questions.solution_md: $7500\left(1 + \dfrac{8 \times 2}{100}\right)$ is the simple-interest amount. With compounding, $A = 7500 \times (1.08)^{2} = 7500 \times 1.1664 = 8748$, which is more than her $8700$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The compound interest on ₹5,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum, compounded yearly, is ₹1,050.

**Reason (R):** The interest for the second year is calculated on ₹5,500, the amount at the end of the first year.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: First year: $500$; second year: $5500 \times \dfrac{10}{100} = 550$; $\text{CI} = 500 + 550 = 1050$. Both are true and R is exactly why the second year's interest is $550$ and not $500$, so the answer is (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On ₹10,000 at 8% per annum for one year, the interest compounded half-yearly is more than the interest compounded yearly.

**Reason (R):** For half-yearly compounding at 8% per annum the rate per period is 8% and there are 2 periods.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: half-yearly gives $10000 \times (1.04)^{2} = 10816$, interest $816$, against $800$ for yearly. R is false: the rate per period is $4\%$ (the yearly rate halved) with $2$ periods. The answer is (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On ₹6,000 at 5% per annum, the compound interest for 1 year is more than the simple interest for 1 year.

**Reason (R):** For the first year the compound interest and the simple interest on the same sum at the same rate are equal.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: R is true: in the first year the interest is on the original principal in both cases. So for 1 year both equal $\dfrac{6000 \times 5}{100} = 300$, and A is false. The answer is (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A machine bought for ₹80,000 that depreciates at 10% per annum is worth ₹64,800 after 2 years.

**Reason (R):** Depreciation is the fall in the value of an article because of use, wear and the passing of time.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $V = 80000 \times (0.9)^{2} = 80000 \times 0.81 = 64800$, so A is true. R is also true (it is the meaning of depreciation), but it does not tell us how the value $64800$ is found, so R is not the explanation. The answer is (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The sum that amounts to ₹7,938 in 2 years at 5% per annum, compounded yearly, is ₹7,200.

**Reason (R):** The sum is found by dividing the amount by $(1.05)^{2}$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $P = \dfrac{7938}{(1.05)^{2}} = \dfrac{7938}{1.1025} = 7200$. A is true, and R gives the exact method that produces it, so R explains A. The answer is (c).

questions.stem_md: In the first year, the compound interest and the simple interest on the same principal at the same rate are equal.
questions.solution_md: During the first year the interest is calculated on the original principal under both methods.

questions.stem_md: At $10\%$ per annum compounded yearly, the amount after 2 years is $P \times 1.2$.
questions.solution_md: The amount is $P \times (1.1)^{2} = 1.21P$. The value $1.2P$ is the simple-interest amount.

questions.stem_md: When interest at 12% per annum is compounded half-yearly, 12% of the current principal is added to it every six months.
questions.solution_md: The rate for six months is $\dfrac{12}{2} = 6\%$, so $6\%$ of the current principal is added every six months.

questions.stem_md: A machine that depreciates at 10% per annum loses the same number of rupees from its value every year.
questions.solution_md: Each year's fall is $10\%$ of the value at the start of that year, and that value keeps getting smaller. For ₹50,000 the falls are ₹5,000, ₹4,500 and ₹4,050 in the first three years.

questions.stem_md: For the same principal, rate and a time of 3 years, the compound interest is more than the simple interest.
questions.solution_md: After the first year, compound interest also earns interest on the interest. For ₹4,000 at $5\%$: $\text{CI} = 630.50$ and $\text{SI} = 600$.

questions.stem_md: A village population that grows by 5% every year increases by more people in the second year than in the first year.
questions.solution_md: The increase each year is $5\%$ of the larger population at the start of that year. For $20000$: first year $1000$, second year $1050$.

questions.stem_md: Compound interest = Amount − ___.
questions.solution_md: $\text{CI} = A - P$: the amount minus the original principal.

questions.stem_md: Interest at 9% per annum compounded half-yearly is calculated at ___ % for each half-year.
The compound interest on ₹4,000 for 2 years at 5% per annum compounded yearly is ₹___.
Interest compounded half-yearly for 3 years has ___ conversion periods.
questions.solution_md: $3 \times 2 = 6$ half-years.

questions.stem_md: A pump costing ₹40,000 loses 10% of its value in the first year and 5% of its new value in the second year. Its value after 2 years is ₹___.
A colony of 20,000 insects grows by 10% in its first month and by 20% of the new number in its second month. The number after 2 months is ___.
Find the compound interest, in rupees, on ₹18,000 for 2 years at 5% per annum, compounded yearly.
questions.solution_md:
$A = 18000 \times \left(1 + \dfrac{5}{100}\right)^{2} = 18000 \times 1.1025 = 19845$.

$\text{CI} = A - P = 19845 - 18000 = 1845$. The compound interest is ₹1,845.

questions.stem_md: Find the amount, in rupees, of ₹25,000 for 1.5 years at 8% per annum, with interest compounded half-yearly.
questions.solution_md:
Rate per half-year $= 4\%$; number of half-years $= 3$.

$A = 25000 \times \left(1 + \dfrac{4}{100}\right)^{3} = 25000 \times 1.124864 = 28121.60$. The amount is ₹28,121.60.

questions.stem_md: The compound interest on a sum for 2 years at 10% per annum is ₹4,200. Find the sum, in rupees.
A sum of ₹8,000 amounts to ₹10,125 in 2 years at a certain rate of compound interest per annum, compounded yearly. Find the rate per cent.
In how many years will ₹12,500 amount to ₹14,060.80 at 4% per annum compound interest?
Find the difference, in rupees, between the compound interest and the simple interest on ₹40,000 for 3 years at 5% per annum.
questions.solution_md:
$\text{CI} = A - P = 46305 - 40000 = 6305$.

$\text{SI} = \dfrac{40000 \times 5 \times 3}{100} = 6000$.

Difference $= 6305 - 6000 = 305$. The difference is ₹305.

questions.stem_md: A generator costing ₹1,25,000 depreciates at 8% per annum. Find its value, in rupees, after 2 years.
Kiran deposits ₹6,000 at 5% per annum for 2 years. Without using the formula, find the interest for each year and the compound interest.

answer.model_answer_md:
Year 1: interest $= \dfrac{6000 \times 5}{100} = 300$; amount $= 6300$.

Year 2: interest $= \dfrac{6300 \times 5}{100} = 315$. Compound interest $= 300 + 315 = 615$, i.e. ₹615.

questions.solution_md: The amount at the end of each year is the principal for the next year.

marking_scheme.step: Interest ₹300 and ₹315 for the two years

questions.stem_md: Find the amount of ₹9,000 for 2 years at 20% per annum, compounded yearly.
questions.solution_md: Use A = P(1 + r/100)^n with n = 2.

questions.stem_md: Find the compound interest on ₹5,000 for 1 year at 12% per annum, compounded half-yearly.

answer.model_answer_md:
Rate per half-year $= 6\%$; half-years $= 2$.

$A = 5000 \times \left(1 + \dfrac{6}{100}\right)^{2} = 5000 \times 1.1236 = 5618$, so $\text{CI} = 5618 - 5000 = 618$, i.e. ₹618.

questions.solution_md: Halve the rate and double the time.

questions.stem_md: A sum amounts to ₹5,290 in 2 years at 15% per annum compounded yearly. Find the sum.
questions.solution_md: Divide the amount by the growth factor.

questions.stem_md: Find the difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on ₹7,500 for 2 years at 8% per annum.
The population of a town is 50,000 and increases by 4% every year. Find its population after 2 years.
questions.solution_md: Growth: multiply by 1 + r/100 every year.

questions.stem_md: A printing machine is valued at ₹36,000 and depreciates at 5% per annum. Find its value after 2 years.
questions.solution_md: Depreciation: multiply by 1 - r/100 every year.

questions.stem_md: Salma says, "The compound interest on ₹1,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum is ₹200 because 10% of ₹1,000 is ₹100 each year." Is she right? Give the correct interest.

answer.model_answer_md:
No. Salma used the same principal ₹1,000 in both years, which is simple interest.

In the second year the principal is $1000 + 100 = 1100$, so the interest is $110$. Correct $\text{CI} = 100 + 110 = 210$, i.e. ₹210.

questions.solution_md: The second year is on ₹1,100, not ₹1,000.

questions.stem_md: Make a table for ₹15,000 invested for 3 years at 6% per annum compounded yearly, showing the principal at the start of each year, the interest for the year and the amount at the end. Hence find the compound interest.
questions.solution_md: Each year's amount is the next year's principal.

questions.stem_md: A bank pays compound interest at 4% for the first year, 5% for the second year and 10% for the third year. Find the amount and the compound interest on ₹20,000 after 3 years.
questions.solution_md: Multiply the principal by the growth factor of each year.

questions.stem_md: A sum of ₹6,400 amounts to ₹7,396 in 2 years, compounded yearly. Find the rate of interest per annum.
questions.solution_md: Write the ratio of amount to principal as a perfect square.

questions.stem_md: In how many years will ₹3,125 amount to ₹5,400 at 20% per annum, with interest compounded yearly? Verify your answer year by year.
questions.solution_md: Compare the ratio with powers of 1.2.

questions.stem_md: The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 6% per annum is ₹36. Find the sum.

answer.model_answer_md:
For 2 years, difference $= P\left(\dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{2}$, so $36 = P \times \left(\dfrac{6}{100}\right)^{2} = 0.0036P$.

$P = \dfrac{36}{0.0036} = 10000$. The sum is ₹10,000.

questions.solution_md: Check: CI = 1,236 and SI = 1,200 on ₹10,000.

questions.stem_md: A culture has 8,000 bacteria. The number grows by 25% every hour. Find the number of bacteria (a) after 1 hour (b) after 2 hours, and (c) the increase in the second hour.
questions.solution_md: Growth of 25% each hour multiplies the number by 1.25.

questions.stem_md:
Meena invests ₹25,000 at 8% per annum, compounded yearly, for 3 years.

(a) Without using the formula, find the interest and the amount at the end of each year.

(b) Find the compound interest she earns.

(c) Find the simple interest on ₹25,000 for 3 years at the same rate, and how much more the compound interest is.
questions.solution_md: Year-by-year amounts, then the formula as a check, then subtract the simple interest.

questions.stem_md:
Girish deposits ₹32,000 in a bank that pays 10% per annum, compounded half-yearly.

(a) Find the rate for each half-year and the number of half-years in 1.5 years.

(b) Find the amount and the compound interest after 1.5 years.

(c) For 1 year, find the compound interest when compounded half-yearly and when compounded yearly, and the difference between them.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Rate per half-year $= 10 \div 2 = 5\%$; number of half-years $= 1.5 \times 2 = 3$.

(b) $A = 32000 \times \left(1 + \dfrac{5}{100}\right)^{3} = 32000 \times 1.157625 = 37044$. Compound interest $= 37044 - 32000 = 5044$, i.e. ₹5,044.

(c) Half-yearly, 1 year: $A = 32000 \times \left(1 + \dfrac{5}{100}\right)^{2} = 32000 \times 1.1025 = 35280$, so $\text{CI} = 35280 - 32000 = 3280$. Yearly: $32000 \times 1.1 = 35200$, so $\text{CI} = 3200$. The difference is $3280 - 3200 = 80$, i.e. ₹80.

questions.solution_md: Halve the rate and double the time; compare with yearly compounding.

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part. Interest is compounded yearly.

(a) A sum amounts to ₹15,435 in 2 years at 5% per annum. Find the sum.

(b) ₹12,500 amounts to ₹16,245 in 2 years. Find the rate per cent per annum.

(c) In how many years will ₹8,000 amount to ₹15,625 at 25% per annum?
questions.solution_md: Divide by the growth factor; express the ratio as a perfect power.

questions.stem_md:
Compare compound interest with simple interest, with yearly compounding.

(a) For ₹24,000 for 2 years at 5% per annum, find the compound interest, the simple interest and the difference.

(b) For ₹30,000 for 3 years at 10% per annum, find the compound interest, the simple interest and the difference.

(c) The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 8% per annum is ₹96. Find the sum.
questions.solution_md: Use the amount formula for CI; for the difference use P(r/100)^2 for 2 years.

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part.

(a) A machine bought for ₹1,60,000 depreciates at 10% per annum. Find its value after 3 years.

(b) The population of a village is 20,000. It grows by 10% in the first year and by 15% in the second year. Find the population after 2 years.

(c) A motorcycle bought for ₹75,000 is worth ₹60,750 after 2 years. Find the yearly rate of depreciation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $V = 160000 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{10}{100}\right)^{3} = 160000 \times 0.729 = 116640$. The value is ₹1,16,640.

(b) $N = 20000 \times \left(1 + \dfrac{10}{100}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{15}{100}\right) = 20000 \times 1.1 \times 1.15 = 25300$. The population is 25,300.

(c) $\left(1 - \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{60750}{75000} = 0.81 = (0.9)^{2}$, so $1 - \dfrac{r}{100} = 0.9$ and $r = 10$. The rate of depreciation is $10\%$ per annum.

questions.solution_md: Depreciation multiplies by 1 - r/100; successive growth rates multiply their factors.

questions.stem_md:
Nirmala has ₹40,000 to invest for 3 years and compares three plans.
Plan A pays simple interest at 6% per annum. Plan B pays compound interest at 5% per annum, compounded yearly. Plan C pays compound interest at 6% per annum, compounded yearly.

(a) Find the interest and the amount from Plan A.

(b) Find the amount and the compound interest from Plan B. Which of A and B is better, and by how much?

(c) Find the compound interest from Plan C, and show that it is more than Plan A by ₹440.64.
questions.solution_md: Same rate, compound interest beats simple interest; a lower rate may not.

marking_scheme.step: (b) CI ₹6,305 and Plan A better by ₹895
